title: Maturity assessments: where does your security really stand, and where should it be?
short: Assess against one model every 12 months, rate only what evidence shows and set a target per function, not one score.
answer: This quarter, pick one model that fits your company and run a five-week assessment that rates each outcome only on evidence you sampled. Set a target per function from your risks, not the top level everywhere, and show management gaps and decisions, not one maturity number.
audience: Heads of security, CISOs, IT leads who own security, and the managing directors they report to

blocks.title: If you only do five things

items.title: Pick one model and keep it.
items.text: Use the model your regulator or sector expects; otherwise NIST CSF 2.0 Profiles with the CIS Controls underneath. Keep the model, scale and scope from year to year, so results compare.

items.title: Scope by business service.
items.text: Assess the services the company can't do without, with their cloud tenants, OT, suppliers and subsidiaries. A CSF Profile can cover the whole organization or one part, such as the financial systems[^csf].

items.title: Rate only what you saw working.
items.text: Interview the people who run each control, then check a sample: settings, tickets, a restore record. NIST's assessment methods are examine, interview and test[^sp80053a]. No evidence means not achieved.

items.title: Set a target per function.
items.text: Decide where each function must be from your risks and duties. NIST encourages higher Tiers when risks or mandates are greater or a cost-benefit analysis supports it[^csf].

items.title: Report gaps and decisions, not a score.
items.text: Show current against target per function, the gaps that matter and what you need decided. A "level 3" is a set of qualities, not a numerical value, as NIST notes[^sp80055].

blocks.title: Choose a model by company type

items.title: Do you run UK essential services?
items.text: Use the NCSC CAF v4.0: 41 outcomes, judged achieved, partially achieved or not achieved[^caf], against the cross-sector Core Profile[^cafcore].

items.title: Do you run energy or OT?
items.text: Use C2M2 v2.1: 356 practices in 10 domains, for IT and OT. DOE's self-evaluation tools are free to any organization; one function takes about a day[^c2m2].

items.title: A German company under 50 staff?
items.text: Book a CyberRisikoCheck (DIN SPEC 27076): an IT service provider checks 27 requirements in a 1 to 2 hour interview and reports a score and ranked recommendations[^crc]. It rests on your answers, so ask for spot checks.

items.title: Is your ISMS built on IT-Grundschutz?
items.text: Use the IT-Grundschutz-Check: interviews plus spot checks against each requirement[^std2002]. Grundschutz++ marks each requirement met, not met or not applicable, with evidence[^std3001].

items.title: Everyone else?
items.text: Build CSF 2.0 Current and Target Profiles in NIST's free template[^profqs], with CIS Controls as the checklist: IG1's 56 safeguards for small firms, IG2's 74 more once you have IT staff and sensitive data[^cisig].

items.title: Week 1: what's in scope, and who answers?
items.text: List services, sites, tenants, OT and suppliers, in the fewest assessments that still give an accurate picture[^c2m2]. Name one contact per area[^std2002].

items.title: Weeks 2 and 3: interviews and samples.
items.text: Interview in pairs, one asking and one taking notes[^std2002]. For each outcome, collect one record and check one live sample.

items.title: Week 4: calibrate and set targets.
items.text: Review the ratings with the interviewees[^c2m2] and one person outside the control's team. Agree targets with management.

items.title: Week 5: report and hand over.
items.text: Present gaps and decisions; the security program sheet turns gaps into a roadmap.

blocks.title: Evidence over self-scoring
items: **Write the rule first.** In the CAF, any "not achieved" indicator normally decides the rating; "achieved" needs all achieved indicators[^caf].

**Sample, don't ask.** Check five leavers' accounts, three servers' patch levels and the last restore record. The BSI suggests checking interview answers against documents, sites and system settings[^std2002].
**Record each rating's source.** Grundschutz++ assigns evidence to each measure and, for automated checks, records tool, time and result[^std3001].
**Count coverage where you can.** CIS's Assessment Specification defines measures and metrics per safeguard, such as how many endpoints implement it[^cas].

blocks.title: Current and target profiles
items: **One row per outcome.** NIST's template has columns for practices, status, rating, priority and goals[^profqs]. Add evidence and an owner.

**Targets per function.** Set Tiers overall or per Function or Category, not per Subcategory[^tiers]. Tiers rate the rigor of risk governance and management[^csf]; per-outcome ratings show whether practices work.
**A floor everywhere.** C2M2 is built so every company can reach MIL1 in all domains[^c2m2]. Go higher where your risks need it.

**Reassess every 12 months** and after major business, technology or threat changes[^c2m2]. NIS2 entities in Germany need procedures to assess their measures' effectiveness (BSIG § 30(2) no. 6)[^bsig].

blocks.title: Presenting results to management
items: **No average.** An overall 2.7 hides a zero in Recover. Show current and target side by side for each function.
**Say how you know.** Name the model version, profile and scope, whether it was self-assessed or independently reviewed, and its limits, as the NCSC asks for CAF results[^cafpage].
**Tie each top gap to a risk.** Give its entry in the risk register (see the risk register sheet), the cost to close it and your recommendation.
**Ask for a decision.** Fund it, accept it with an end date or defer it. Put progress on the security metrics sheet's quarterly page.
**Show what moved.** Next year, show what changed and why, on the same scale.

blocks.title: External assessor or your own team
items: **Run the yearly cycle yourself.** Your people know where the evidence is; C2M2 is built for facilitated self-evaluation[^c2m2].
**Buy independence where it counts.** Independent audit or testing generally gives more confidence, the NCSC says[^cafpage]. Use it every 2 to 3 years, never from the firm selling the fixes.
**Keep reviewers out of the line.** NIS2 digital providers need reviewers with audit competence outside the reviewed area's line of authority[^nis2ir].

**Check the licenses.** CIS's Controls and Assessment Specification allow non-commercial use within your organization[^casterms]; consultants using CSAT on you need a CIS SecureSuite consulting membership[^csat].

blocks.title: What changed in 2026
items: **The UK set a cross-sector CAF minimum.** The NCSC's Core Profile, published 30 October 2026, sets the expected level for each CAF v4.0 outcome against moderately sophisticated attackers[^cafcore].

**Grundschutz++ drops "partially".** BSI-Standard 300-1, dated 20 October 2026, marks each requirement met, not met or not applicable[^std3001]; the IT-Grundschutz-Check also allowed partially[^std2002]. The BSI plans performance indicators for the method's requirements by 31 March 2027[^gspp].

blocks.title: What you can skip
items: **A second framework for comparison.** Map once through informative references to ISO/IEC 27001 or SP 800-53[^profqs].
**Tiers for every Subcategory.** NIST says Function or Category level gives a better picture[^tiers].
**Peer benchmark scores.** Ratings from different assessors, scopes and scales don't compare. Compare yourself with last year.
**A maturity platform before the first cycle.** NIST's spreadsheet template and your ticket system will do[^profqs].

blocks.title: Mistakes that cost the most
items: **Scoring the paper.** The BSI rates "yes" only for measures implemented fully, effectively and appropriately[^std2002], not for a signed policy.
**Chasing level 5 everywhere.** It costs most where risk is lowest; DOE calls the top level in all domains not typically optimal[^c2m2].
**Buying a score.** Tools that turn questionnaires or external scans into a maturity number measure answers or the perimeter, not practice.
**Taking "implemented" for "works".** CIS's specification checks only whether a safeguard is implemented[^cas]. Test a restore or an alert.
**Changing the yardstick.** A new model, scale or scope each year breaks the trend.

blocks.title: What this looks like at your size

columns.title: Small team, no security staff
items: In Germany, book a CyberRisikoCheck[^crc] each year, ideally with a provider other than the one running your IT.
Elsewhere, rate yourself against CIS IG1 with one piece of evidence per safeguard.
Take the managing directors through the top five gaps in one hour.

columns.title: Growing, with IT or security staff
items: Build Current and Target Profiles per CSF Function in NIST's template, with CIS IG2 as the checklist.
Have someone outside IT operations, such as internal audit, recheck a sample.
Finish the assessment before budget planning starts.

columns.title: Enterprise or regulated
items: Use the model your regulator expects: the CAF Core Profile for UK essential services, C2M2 for energy and OT.
Assess each subsidiary or business unit with the same scale and evidence rules.
Report independent reviews to management, as Regulation 2024/2690 requires of digital providers[^nis2ir].

changes.text: First draft, based on NIST CSF 2.0 and its Profiles and Tiers guides, NCSC CAF v4.0 and its Core Profile, C2M2 v2.1, CIS Controls v8.1, BSI-Standards 200-2 and 300-1 and the BSI's CyberRisikoCheck.
